claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic interplay between mechanical wear and passivating-oxide reformation.
Selective elemental segregation during wear promotes rapid self-healing of the surface film.
Dynamic oxide self-healing mitigates both wear and corrosion damage.
The initial alloy is homogeneously mixed and has uniformly distributed refractory and oxidizable elements.
The alloy has a stable as-deposited microstructure.
Wear-induced exposure of fresh substrate followed by re-oxidation produces a transient, selectively enriched oxide or hydroxide film.
Elements with high oxygen affinity mediate selective enrichment of the surface film.
Mechanical wear removes the protective oxide layer and exposes fresh alloy surface.
The high-entropy composition promotes surface segregation of passivating species such as Cr- or Mn-like elements.
The segregated passivating species rapidly regenerate a protective oxide after wear.
Dynamic oxide regeneration balances wear removal and corrosion so that coupled degradation is less than the simple sum of the separate effects.
Relative to an alloy with slower oxide reformation, the tested alloy will have a lower net degradation rate.
The tested alloy will show lower corrosion current density than the baseline.
The tested alloy will show decreased steady-state wear depth relative to the baseline.
The wear and corrosion contributions will be mutually compensating.
The proposed behavior should hold under moderate mechanical and chemical attack when the oxide can continually regenerate.
The mechanism may fail at very high wear rates or in environments aggressive enough to prevent oxide formation.
Pre-oxidizing the alloy to form an inert scale will prevent or substantially suppress dynamic oxide reformation during sliding.
